questions.q: What is the key difference between a resource block and a data block?
options: A data block always runs before a resource block
A resource block creates and manages a lifecycle; a data block only reads existing information and manages nothing
A data block can only be used with AWS, never Azure
There is no real difference — they are interchangeable
questions.explain: A resource block creates something and manages its full lifecycle (create, update, destroy). A data block only looks up and returns attributes of something it does not manage.

questions.q: In data "azurerm_resource_group" "shared_networking" { ... }, how would you reference its location elsewhere in the configuration?
options: azurerm_resource_group.shared_networking.location
data.azurerm_resource_group.shared_networking.location
shared_networking.location
var.shared_networking.location
questions.explain: Data source references follow data.<type>.<local name>.<attribute> — the same pattern as resource references, prefixed with "data" to mark it as a lookup.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's AWS example use a data source to find an AMI instead of hardcoding an AMI ID?
options: Hardcoded AMI IDs are not supported by Terraform at all
A hardcoded ID would go stale as the vendor publishes newer images; the data source looks up the current match at plan time
Data sources are required for every AWS resource
AMI IDs can only be read through a data block, never written directly
questions.explain: A vendor-published AMI changes over time as new versions are released. Hardcoding an ID freezes you on a version that eventually goes stale, while a data source resolves to whatever currently matches the filter.

questions.q: When would you reach for a data source instead of a resource block?
options: When you want Terraform to delete the resource on the next apply
When something is managed outside this configuration, but you still need to read its attributes
When a resource type has no required arguments
Only when working with AWS, never Azure
questions.explain: Data sources are for infrastructure you don't own or control — managed by another team, another configuration, or a vendor — that you still need to read values from.

questions.q: Can Terraform modify or destroy something described by a data block?
options: Yes, if the data block's arguments change
No — a data block only reads; it never creates, modifies, or destroys anything
Only during terraform destroy
Only if no resource block references it
questions.explain: Data blocks are read-only by design. Terraform never creates, modifies, or destroys whatever a data source looks up.
